extracted.intended_audience: scholars, researchers and graduate students in pragmatics, linguistics, and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic/practical framework for analyzing and producing humorous texts using Relevance Theory (RT): identifies cognitive-pragmatic mechanisms, inferential strategies, classifications (jokes, puns, stand-up, translation, media), and contextual/non-propositional constraints that determine humorous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive and communicative principles of relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Human cognition is geared to the maximization of relevance (cognitive principle). Every utterance conveys a presumption of its eventual relevance (communicative principle); hearers expect interpretation to be worth the effort and to yield reward (in humor: amusement/entertainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the baseline evaluative metric: a humorous utterance is judged by whether it produces sufficient cognitive/affective payoff to justify the extra mental effort (e.g. resolving ambiguities, alternative referents, puns). Examples: jokes are 'informationally irrelevant' yet expected to reward with amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker prediction of hearer inferential strategies (mind-reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers can hold more or less precise expectations about which inferential strategies and contextual information the hearer will access to interpret a joke (which sense of ambiguous words will be selected, which referents for indexicals, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing/analysing humor, evaluate the degree to which the speaker successfully anticipates hearer accessibility and inferential steps; effective jokes exploit predictable hearer choices to create later clash/incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearer's ranking of candidate interpretations by relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearers assess multiple possible interpretations for the same input and unconsciously rank them according to balance of positive cognitive effects vs mental effort, automatically opting for the most relevant one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor often exploits this automatic preference by inducing an initially favoured interpretation that must later be replaced by a less likely one; evaluate how well the joke sets up and then disconfirms the preferred reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-phase comprehension: decoding (logical form) then inference (explicature/implicature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehension involves decoding a grammatical logical form (context-free) and then inferentially turning it into a contextualized explicature and possibly implicatures; utterances underdetermine ultimate interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how humorous texts use the gap between coded utterance and intended interpretation; successful humor manipulates decoding vs inferencing (e.g. leaves unarticulated slots, requires enrichment or conceptual adjustment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferential strategies exploited for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferential operations used to derive intended interpretations include reference assignment (for indexicals/pronouns), disambiguation, free enrichment (filling unarticulated slots), and conceptual adjustment (creating ad hoc concepts broader or narrower than coded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or crafting humor, identify which inferential operations are invoked and how they are manipulated (e.g. disambiguation of 'bank' or ad hoc narrowing as in 'drinks too much'). These strategies are primary tools for generating incongruity and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution via stretch-by-stretch clashes (MGI/SCI schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be generated during cumulative processing when an initial stretch (MGI: multiple graded interpretations) leads to a strong accessible interpretation that is later disconfirmed by a subsequent part foregrounding a covert single covert interpretation (SCI), producing incongruity and its resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MGI/SCI to evaluate jokes with setup+punchline structure: check that the MGI establishes a dominant reading and that the SCI part legitimately licenses the alternative reading and provides the cognitive effect (amusement) that offsets effort. Example: pregnancy vs mother moving in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curcó-style key assumption vs target assumption clash
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaker can lead hearer to entertain a strongly implicated premise (key assumption) that clashes with an accessible—though previously unaccessed—assumption (target assumption), producing humor when both are entertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether a joke creates two contradictory propositional contents (key vs target) and how the clash is revealed; evaluate strength of the implicated premise and accessibility of the target assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersecting Circles Model (three Circles classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are classified by intersections of three Circles: (1) Utterance interpretation (manipulation of inferential strategies), (2) Make-sense frame (construction of a situation/schema/script), and (3) Cultural frame (collective/stereotypical representations). The three Circles yield seven types of jokes depending on which Circles combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying jokes, identify which Circle(s) are active and how their interaction generates humor (e.g. Make-sense frame + Utterance interpretation as in the 'contacts' policeman joke). The model emphasizes combined mechanisms rather than single-cause labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-sense frame (frame/schema/script building)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearer builds an effort-saving mental situation or scenario that constrains interpretations (frame/schema/script) and aids accessibility and disambiguation during joke processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively a joke constructs a make-sense frame that supports an initial reading and how that frame is later exploited or overturned to create incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning taxonomy: sense-pair types
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning involves various pairings of concepts enabled by a punning element: homonymy, polysemy, metaphorical vs literal juxtaposition, perfect or imperfect homophony, paronymy, homography, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the linguistic relationship enabling the pun (e.g. polysemy vs homophony) and how those relations are leveraged to produce parallel senses and cognitive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns: three-label classification (structure, sense relationship, inferential strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each pun should receive three labels: Label 1 (punning structure: two senses in parallel; one sense then another; one sense present other absent; both senses absent), Label 2 (sense relationship: homophony, polysemy, paronymy, etc.), Label 3 (inferential strategy: logical form, disambiguation, conceptual adjustment, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-label system to uniquely delimit pun types; evaluate where senses are encoded/activated and which inferential operations the hearer must perform (examples: period joke, Rubik's cube joke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up comedy: personal vs collective mental-representation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up effectiveness often derives from manipulating the audience's personal vs collective status of mental representations—reminding individuals that certain 'private' beliefs/behaviours are actually collective—leading to mutual manifestness and laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess stand-up material by how it shifts representations from personal to collective (or challenges/strengthens stereotypes) and the degree to which this shift produces bonding, identity effects, and amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor translation scenarios (cultural, semantic, pragmatic: inferential steps & balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translatability depends on four parameters (combined into a 16-case chart): Cultural scenario (shared cultural assumptions), Semantic scenario (parallel coding options in languages), Pragmatic scenario A (preserving predicted inferential steps), Pragmatic scenario B (preserving balance of cognitive effects and effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating jokes, evaluate which scenarios are preserved/altered; translators may change semantic content to preserve inferential steps and/or the effects/effort balance (example given: replacing polysemy to keep pragmatic/inferential effect). Use the 16-case matrix to categorize translation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended relevance formula: non-propositional constraints and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to enrich the RT formula (cognitive effects vs mental effort) by adding positive/negative contextual constraints and positive/negative non-propositional effects (feelings, emotions, impressions). Successful humorous communication requires the sum of cognitive effects + positive contextual constraints + positive non-propositional effects to exceed mental effort + negative contextual constraints + negative non-propositional effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the extended formula to judge humor success beyond propositional content—include phatic, social, interactive, and affective payoffs as part of the benefit side of the balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of contextual/non-propositional constraints affecting humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables that can be positive or negative constraints/effects include: (a) suitability of uttering a joke, (b) hearer's background knowledge and beliefs, (c) interlocutor's sex, (d) interlocutor's sense of humor, (e) relationship between interlocutors, (f) group size, (g) interlocutor's mood, (h) culture and ethnicity, (i) situational factors (e.g. serious meeting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor by how these factors modulate accessibility, offense/risk, or non-propositional payoff; note that same factor can be both constraint and effect (e.g. ethnic origin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous irony: echoic, dissociative, and affective-attitude inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony comprehension involves (a) echoing a belief attributed to someone else, (b) being echoic, and (c) involving a dissociative attitude; correct interpretation requires inferring also a second-order affective attitude (feelings/emotions) that signals whether the dissociation is humorous (play frame) or aggressive/critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze ironic utterances by distinguishing propositional dissociation from affective attitude; evaluate whether the affective attitude licenses humor versus offense or serious critique (examples illustrate humorous vs non-humorous outcomes depending on inferred feelings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous narratives: long-form constraints (repetition, character-centered expectations, stereotypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: RT analyses of long narratives are limited because typical joke strategies (incongruity-resolution) are hard to maintain across hundreds of pages; narrative humor often relies on repeated salient connotations, established character images, and stereotypes that condition readers' search for relevance and later implicatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-form narrative humor, evaluate how early-established expectations about characters and repeated connotations create opportunities for later incongruity and humorous implicatures; be cautious applying short-joke RT analyses directly to long narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational humor: single-speaker vs co-constructed multi-party mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversational humor in groups can be (1) a single speaker telling a joke to several interlocutors (parallel one-to-one relevance processing) or (2) co-constructed multi-party humor where interlocutors collaboratively add turns and complete others' initiations to achieve humorous effects that cannot be located in a single utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing conversational humor, determine whether humour is generated by a univocal coded utterance or by interactive co-construction; evaluate demands on shared context, timing, and collaborative inferencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media/cartoon/advertising technique: forcing parallel literal/idiomatic (or literal/metaphoric) interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers and cartoonists can alter normal relevance-based interpretation by using images to force readers to entertain parallel literal and idiomatic/metaphoric readings of the same text, producing incongruity, increased attention, and possible amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate media humour by how well the visual/verbal combination levels accessibility of an otherwise unlikely literal reading (e.g. 'No se quede colgado' with image of man hanging) and whether this yields sufficient cognitive/affective payoff to justify added effort.
